warmup.q: A PostgreSQL server keeps 128 MB of table pages in memory. Every night, a report reads all of a 60 GB table once, page by page from start to end. What happens to the pages of the busy payments table that were in memory?
options: They're all thrown out, because the report reads far more pages than memory holds
Most of them stay: a big read from start to end reuses a small ring of memory instead of filling all of it
They stay, because PostgreSQL never throws out a page that was used in the last hour
The report fails, because the table is bigger than the memory
warmup.why: A cache that always throws out the page used longest ago would lose everything to a report like that, which is why the first option tempts. PostgreSQL gives a read of a whole table bigger than a quarter of its page memory its own small ring of pages, so the report keeps reusing the same few hundred kilobytes. The last Try it of this lesson measures it. There's no rule based on time, and a read never fails for being bigger than the memory.

sections.h: Keeping busy pages in memory: the buffer pool
sections.html:
Every query, every question a program asks the database, reads pages. Looking up one payment by its id reads a few pages of an index (a lookup structure that finds rows without reading the whole table) and one table page. A monthly report reads thousands. Reading an 8 KB page from an NVMe SSD, the fast kind of drive in most laptops and servers, takes about 100 microseconds. Reading it from RAM, the computer's memory, takes well under one. And queries keep coming back to the same pages: the top of every index, today's payments, the table of card limits. So a database keeps copies of pages in memory, and serves repeat reads from there.

The desk from the opening is the picture: the shelf is the drive, the desk is memory, and each book is a page. It breaks in one way. A desk holds books of every size, while each place in memory holds exactly one 8 KB page, so any page fits anywhere.

Version 1 is a HashMap<Int, ByteArray>, a hash map that finds a page's bytes by its page number in one step, filled on every read. It works until the database is bigger than RAM, which most are: a 2 TB table (two trillion bytes) doesn't fit in a server's 64 GB (64 billion bytes) of memory. The cache needs a fixed size, and once it's full, something has to leave.

Version 2 is the buffer pool: a fixed number of page-sized places in memory, called frames, plus a hash map from page number to frame, called the page table. To read page 42, look it up in the page table. If it's there, that's a hit, and no I/O (input and output, a trip to the drive) happens. If not, it's a miss: the pool picks a frame, reads page 42 from the drive into it, and records it in the page table. When every frame already holds a page, the pool first picks a victim, a page to throw out, or evict. The figure shows the picture this whole lesson builds on.

In PostgreSQL, the buffer pool is shared_buffers, one block of shared memory: memory that several processes, running programs, can all read and write. PostgreSQL starts one process, called a backend, for each program connected to it, and every backend uses the same pool. The default is 128 MB: 16,384 frames of 8 KB. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) runs a query and reports each step it took (lesson 7 of this track reads it in full). For each step it shows shared hit for pages found in the pool and shared read for misses, and PostgreSQL 18 shows these by default.

Why not let the operating system cache the file instead? The kernel, the core of the operating system, already keeps a page cache, its own copy of file data in memory. (The page cache, writeback and fsync, lesson 9 of the Operating systems track, opens it up.) And mmap can make a file look like part of a program's memory, so the kernel loads pages as they're touched (Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer, lesson 7 of that track). Some systems lean on that. Bitcask, from the first lesson of this track, does, and PostgreSQL partly does, as the last section shows.

But the database knows things the kernel doesn't. It knows which pages a query is using right now. It knows that a changed page must not reach the drive before the log record that describes it (lesson 6 of this track). And it knows that a big scan's pages won't be read again. A 2022 paper by Crotty, Leis and Pavlo shows what goes wrong when a database leaves these choices to the kernel through mmap. The kernel can write a changed page back at any moment. Any read of memory can stall while the kernel fetches a missing page. And a failed read arrives as a signal that interrupts the program, not as an error it can check. In their tests, mmap was 2 to 20 times slower than direct I/O, reading files without the kernel's page cache, once memory filled up.

So the database runs its own pool, and each frame carries a little bookkeeping: a pin count, a dirty flag and a usage count. The next three sections add them one at a time.

try.title: Count hits and reads
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. Docker runs programs in containers, each with a private view of the computer, and this starts PostgreSQL 18 in one. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's program for typing commands, with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.

Create a payments table of 200,000 rows (1,280 pages) and run VACUUM, PostgreSQL's cleanup command, on it. Otherwise the first scan also writes a few status bits into every page, which PostgreSQL does the first time it reads freshly inserted rows, and the numbers get noisy.

Throw the table's pages out of shared_buffers with pg_buffercache_evict_relation, new in PostgreSQL 18. (pg_buffercache is an add-on that ships with PostgreSQL and shows what the pool holds.) Then run the same count twice. Predict the Buffers line of each run.

code.title: psql
code.html: CREATE TABLE payments AS SELECT g AS id, 'card-' || (g % 5000) AS card, (g % 997) * 100 AS amount_cents FROM generate_series(1, 200000) g; VACUUM payments; SELECT pg_relation_size('payments') / 8192 AS pages; SELECT buffers_evicted FROM pg_buffercache_evict_relation('payments'); EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM payments; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM payments;

try.expect:
The first run misses on every page, and the second hits on every page:

 Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared read=1280
   I/O Timings: shared read=0.151
   ->  Seq Scan on payments (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
         Buffers: shared read=1280
...
 Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=1280
   ->  Seq Scan on payments (actual rows=200000.00 loops=1)
         Buffers: shared hit=1280

(output trimmed). The I/O Timings line is there because the course's setup turns on track_io_timing, a setting that times every read. Notice how small the read time is: 1,280 "reads" in about 0.15 ms. Those pages were still in the Linux page cache inside Docker's Linux machine, so no SSD was involved. The last section comes back to that.

video.title: The buffer pool: a desk with four places

sections.h: A page in use must stay: pins, and pages that changed
sections.html:
A miss can throw out any frame, and that's dangerous. Query A fetches page 12 and starts reading a row at byte 8,144 of its frame. Query B misses on page 99, the pool picks page 12's frame as the victim, and reads page 99 over it. Query A's next read returns page 99's bytes as if they were its row.

Version 1 adds an inUse flag to each frame: set it on fetch, clear it when done, and never evict a frame with the flag set. It breaks as soon as two queries use one page. A and B both fetch page 12, A finishes and clears the flag, and the frame is evicted while B is still reading it.

Version 2 is a count. fetch adds one to the frame's pin count, and unpin takes one away. On the desk, a pin is a friend's hand on the book: "I'm reading this, leave it." The rule is absolute: a frame with a pin count above zero is never a victim. Two queries reading the same busy page each hold a pin, and the page stays until both are done.

The second problem is changes. An UPDATE, the command in SQL (the language programs use to talk to a database) that changes a row, changes bytes in the frame, not on the drive. Writing the page to the drive on every change is safe and slow: a card's daily-total row updated 500 times a minute would cost 500 page writes a minute. So the pool marks the frame dirty, meaning it differs from the copy on the drive, and writes it once, when the frame is about to be reused. (Lesson 6 of this track adds the other moment, the checkpoint.) The caller reports its change through unpin(pageId, dirty = true). The flag is sticky: a later caller that unpins without changes must not clear it, or the earlier change is lost when the frame is reused.

A pin is a promise to give the page back, and promises get forgotten. A code path that fetches a page and returns early on an error, without unpinning, leaves that frame pinned forever. Leak enough pins and every frame is pinned, so a miss has nowhere to go. Your lab throws NoFreeFrameException, and PostgreSQL raises no unpinned buffers available. On the desk, it's friends who keep a hand on books they finished with long ago: nothing goes wrong until every book is held down. PostgreSQL releases a backend's pins when a query ends or fails, which is one reason you rarely see that error.

A pin isn't a lock, either. A lock lets one user at a time change something, and makes the others wait; a pin only says "keep this page in memory". PostgreSQL also takes a short content lock on the page while it reads or changes bytes in it (shared for reading, exclusive for writing). It must hold a pin before it may take the lock. Tidying a page, as VACUUM did in Pages, tuples and heap files, needs an exclusive lock and must be the only pin on the page. It moves row bytes, and another reader may be in the middle of them.

Pins say which pages must stay. When a miss needs a frame, the pool still has to choose among the others. Next, we'll see how.

try.title: Catch a pin in the act
steps: A cursor lets a query stop in the middle and hand over its rows a few at a time. Open one on payments inside a transaction (BEGIN), and fetch three rows.
While the cursor is open, ask pg_buffercache which pages of payments are pinned. Predict: how many?
Move the cursor 300 rows on (a page holds 157 of these rows) and ask again. Then COMMIT, which ends the transaction and closes the cursor, and count the pins once more.

code.title: psql
code.html: BEGIN; DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT * FROM payments; FETCH 3 FROM c; SELECT relblocknumber, pinning_backends FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('payments') AND pinning_backends > 0; MOVE 300 IN c; SELECT relblocknumber, pinning_backends FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('payments') AND pinning_backends > 0; COMMIT; SELECT count(*) AS pinned FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('payments') AND pinning_backends > 0;

try.expect:
relblocknumber | pinning_backends
----------------+------------------
              0 |                1
              1 |                1
...
 relblocknumber | pinning_backends
----------------+------------------
              1 |                1
              2 |                1
...
 pinned
--------
      0

While the cursor sits on row 3, your backend pins page 0, which it's reading, and page 1, which PostgreSQL 18's scan has already read ahead. After 300 more rows, the pins have moved to pages 1 and 2. COMMIT closes the cursor, and every pin is released.

sections.h: Choosing which page leaves: from LRU to the clock sweep
sections.html:
When a miss finds no free frame, which page should leave? A good choice keeps the pages that will be read again soon. A bad one throws out the top page of an index, the page where every lookup in it starts, and the next query reads it straight back.

Version 1 picks a random unpinned frame. It's cheap, and sooner or later it evicts the busiest page in the pool. Version 2 is first in, first out: evict the page that was loaded longest ago. That's exactly the index's top page, loaded at startup and used ever since.

Version 3 is the opening's rule, LRU, least recently used: evict the page whose last use is oldest. It's the right idea, and costly to build. A real LRU keeps all frames in a list ordered by last use, so every hit moves a frame to the front. Every read becomes a write to one shared list. A server's processor has many cores, parts that each run one thread, one path of work, at a time. With dozens of cores hitting the cache, the lock on that list is where they all queue.

Version 4, CLOCK, gets most of LRU's benefit at a fraction of the cost. Picture the frames on a clock face with one hand. A hit only marks its own frame as recently used. When a victim is needed, the hand moves frame by frame. A marked frame loses its mark and gets a second chance, and the first unmarked frame is the victim. On the desk, each book carries a paper tab. When you need room, you walk round the desk from where you stopped last time, peel the tab off each book that has one, and send back the first book with none.

PostgreSQL's clock sweep gives each frame a few tabs instead of one:

  • Each frame has a usage count. Loading a page sets it to 1, and every pin adds 1, up to a cap of 5.
  • To find a victim, the hand moves on from where it last stopped. It skips pinned frames without touching them. An unpinned frame with a count above 0 loses one, and the hand moves on. The first unpinned frame at 0 is the victim, and the hand stops right past it.
  • If the hand passes every frame and finds only pinned ones, PostgreSQL gives up with no unpinned buffers available.

A hit costs one counter update on the frame itself. PostgreSQL packs a frame's pin count, usage count and flags into one 32-bit number. It updates that number with compare-and-swap: one processor instruction that changes a value only if it still holds what you expect. That's the same operation as Java's AtomicInteger.compareAndSet, so a hit takes no lock at all. Pages used often build up credits and survive several sweeps; pages touched once drain to 0 and leave first. The cap keeps that fair. Without it, a page read a million times this morning would need a million sweeps to leave this afternoon.

Before the victim's frame is reused, a dirty page is written back to the drive, exactly once. A clean one is dropped, since the drive already has the same bytes. The stepper runs one sweep with PostgreSQL's rules, and the lab asks you to build it.

The clock keeps busy pages and lets idle ones go. One kind of query can still beat it, and next we'll meet it.

try.title: Watch usage counts climb to 5
steps: Look at the usage counts of the payments pages now. Predict: what number, after one read and one hit?
Run the count once more and look again. Then run it four more times, and look a third time. \g /dev/null runs a query and throws its answer away.
Look at the whole pool with pg_buffercache_usage_counts(). How many of the 16,384 frames are still unused (usage 0, not dirty, not pinned)?

code.title: psql
code.html: SELECT usagecount, count(*) AS buffers FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('payments') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; SELECT count(*) FROM payments \g /dev/null SELECT usagecount, count(*) AS buffers FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('payments') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; -- four more times, then look again SELECT count(*) FROM payments \g /dev/null SELECT count(*) FROM payments \g /dev/null SELECT count(*) FROM payments \g /dev/null SELECT count(*) FROM payments \g /dev/null SELECT usagecount, count(*) AS buffers FROM pg_buffercache WHERE relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode('payments') GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1; SELECT * FROM pg_buffercache_usage_counts();

usagecount | buffers
------------+---------
          2 |    1277

 usagecount | buffers
------------+---------

One read set each count to 1, the hit made it 2, and each scan adds 1 until the cap of 5. The three pages one higher are the ones the cursor in the previous Try it pinned again. sections.h: One big scan against the busy pages: the ring buffer
sections.html:
One sequential scan, a read of a whole table from its first page to its last, can wreck all of this. Picture a nightly report over a 60 GB table of settlements, the company's daily payouts to each shop. It touches 7.8 million pages, exactly once each. Under LRU, every one of them is briefly the most recently used page in the pool. So within seconds, the pages the payments app reads all day are gone, and every lookup misses. This is sequential flooding: the opening's student leafing through every book on the shelf once, and clearing the desk to do it.

CLOCK alone doesn't stop it. Millions of misses push the hand round the pool again and again. A page at the full count of 5 is gone after five passes, and a big scan makes those passes quickly.

PostgreSQL's answer is a ring buffer. A sequential scan of a table bigger than a quarter of shared_buffers doesn't take frames from the whole pool. It gets a small private ring of frames and keeps reusing them, so the rest of the pool doesn't notice the scan. On the desk, it's a corner set aside for the books you'll open once: each new one replaces the last, and nothing else moves.

The buffer manager is the part of PostgreSQL's code that runs the pool, and its README, the design notes next to that code, gives 256 KB for scans. In PostgreSQL 18, the code starts there and enlarges the ring to fit the reads it keeps waiting on the drive at once (the last section explains those). The ring stops growing at a limit on how many pins one backend may hold. In the Try it, the ring comes to 94 pages, about 750 KB, for a scan of 7,680 pages. VACUUM gets its own ring, sized by vacuum_buffer_usage_limit. Bulk writes such as COPY, which loads many rows from a file, get 16 MB. Only these operations use a ring. An index scan that walks a huge range of keys goes through the normal pool, and can still push busy pages out.

The ring protects PostgreSQL's own pool. But PostgreSQL isn't the only one keeping pages in memory. Next, we'll find a second copy of every page it reads.

try.title: Scan 60 MB without flushing the pool
steps: Create a 60 MB settlements table (7,680 pages: nearly half of the 128 MB pool, and well over a quarter of it). Throw its pages out of the pool, so the scan starts cold, with nothing in memory.

PostgreSQL can split a big scan across several helper processes, called parallel workers. Turn them off for this session, so one process does the scan with one ring. Make sure payments is fully in the pool by counting it once.
Scan settlements, then count how many pages of each table are in the pool. Predict both numbers first.

code.title: psql
code.html: CREATE TABLE settlements AS SELECT g AS id, 'batch-' || (g % 365) AS batch, g % 100000 AS amount_cents FROM generate_series(1, 1200000) g; VACUUM settlements; SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('settlements')) AS size, pg_relation_size('settlements') / 8192 AS pages; SELECT buffers_evicted FROM pg_buffercache_evict_relation('settlements'); SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0; SELECT count(*) FROM payments; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM settlements; SELECT c.relname, count(b.bufferid) AS cached_pages FROM pg_class c LEFT JOIN pg_buffercache b ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid) AND b.relforknumber = 0 WHERE c.relname IN ('payments', 'settlements') GROUP BY c.relname ORDER BY c.relname;

try.expect:
The scan reads all 7,680 pages, yet almost none of them stay, and payments loses nothing:

 Aggregate (actual rows=1.00 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared read=7680
...
   relname   | cached_pages
-------------+--------------
 payments    |         1280
 settlements |           94

(output trimmed). The 94 pages are the ring. With parallel workers on, each of the three processes gets its own ring, and about 280 pages stay. Try the same scan on a table under a quarter of the pool, like payments, and every page stays in the pool. Leave the database running for the last Try it.

sections.h: Two caches for one page, and PostgreSQL 18 starts reading ahead itself
sections.html:
PostgreSQL reads its files with ordinary system calls, the requests a program makes to the kernel. So every page passes through the kernel's page cache on its way into shared_buffers, as the figure shows, and one page can sit in both caches. That's on purpose. The docs suggest about 25% of RAM for shared_buffers and say more than 40% is unlikely to help, because PostgreSQL also relies on the operating system's cache. It also means a shared read in EXPLAIN is a system call (pread, which reads bytes at a given position), not always a trip to the SSD. In the first Try it, 1,280 "reads" took 0.15 ms in all.

Most database engines skip the kernel's copy. They open their data files with O_DIRECT, a flag that tells the kernel to move data straight between the drive and the program's memory, so the page cache never holds it. MySQL, another popular free database, does this for InnoDB, its storage engine, by default on Linux (in MySQL 8.4, innodb_flush_method is O_DIRECT where the system supports it). The pool can then take most of the RAM, and nothing is cached twice. The price is that the engine must now do what the kernel did for it: read ahead, merge neighbouring reads, and keep many reads waiting on the drive at once.

PostgreSQL 18, released in September 2025, took the first step. Its asynchronous I/O lets a backend ask early for the pages it will need soon, and work on the ones that have arrived while the others are on their way. The setting io_method picks who carries out those reads. worker, the default, hands them to I/O worker processes (io_workers, 3 by default). io_uring uses Linux's io_uring, a way to hand the kernel many reads at once (lesson 11 of the Operating systems track), when PostgreSQL is built with it, as the Docker image is. sync is the old way, one read at a time. It covers reads only, such as sequential scans and VACUUM; writes stay as they were.

How much it helps depends on how long each read waits. pganalyze, a company that makes tools for watching PostgreSQL, timed a cold SELECT count(*) of a 3.5 GB table on Amazon's network storage, rated at 20,000 reads and writes a second (io2 EBS). It took 15.1 s with sync, 10.1 s with worker and 5.7 s with io_uring. On a laptop the gap is smaller, because the scan is mostly work for the processor: in the Try it, worker beat sync by about a fifth. And in Docker you can't try io_uring at all. Docker's default safety rules (its seccomp profile) block the system calls it needs, and PostgreSQL refuses to start with FATAL: could not setup io_uring queue: Operation not permitted.

All of this makes reading a page cheaper. None of it helps a query that must read every page to find one row, and that's the next lesson's problem.

try.title: Scan cold with worker, then with sync
steps: In the same psql session, create a 731 MB table of 10 million rows (about 15 seconds). Run VACUUM on it, then CHECKPOINT, which makes PostgreSQL write every changed page to the drive, so the table's pages are clean.

Run the rest of the block. It checks io_method, throws the table out of shared_buffers, and asks the kernel to drop the file from its page cache (dd ... iflag=nocache count=0, run inside the container through \!). Then it scans twice: cold, and with the kernel's copy warm. Note I/O Timings and Execution Time.

Switch to sync: run ALTER SYSTEM SET io_method = 'sync';, quit psql with \q, restart with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml restart db, open psql again and run the block from SHOW io_method on. Predict which cold scan is slower, and what happens to I/O Timings.
Put the default back with ALTER SYSTEM RESET io_method; and one more restart. When you're done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v.

code.title: psql
code.html: CREATE TABLE scan_me AS SELECT g AS id, g % 1000 AS merchant_id, (g % 997) * 100 AS amount_cents, md5(g::text) AS ref FROM generate_series(1, 10000000) g; VACUUM scan_me; CHECKPOINT; SHOW io_method; SET max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0; SELECT pg_relation_filepath('scan_me') AS f \gset \setenv F :f SELECT buffers_evicted FROM pg_buffercache_evict_relation('scan_me'); \! dd if=/var/lib/postgresql/18/docker/$F iflag=nocache count=0 status=none EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM scan_me; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF, TIMING OFF) SELECT count(*) FROM scan_me;

With the default, worker (output trimmed):

After the switch to sync:

Cold, worker took 370 to 410 ms in our runs, and sync 460 to 500 ms. Under sync the backend waits for every read itself, 130 to 170 ms in all. Under worker its own wait is a few milliseconds, because the I/O workers did the waiting ahead of it. So under asynchronous I/O, EXPLAIN understates how much reading happened. Warm, the kernel serves every read from its cache, and the scan is processor work: counting 10 million rows. The 94 hits are the ring left by the previous scan. Docker's simulated disk on a laptop is fast; on network storage the cold gap grows, as pganalyze measured. Your times differ.

refs.title: Matsunobu, Dong, Lee: MyRocks, LSM-tree database storage engine serving Facebook's social graph (PVLDB 2020)
Andy Pavlo: Databases in 2025, a year in review

opening:
Picture yourself studying for an exam at a small desk. It holds four open books, and the rest sit on a shelf across the room. A glance at the desk takes a second; a walk to the shelf takes a minute. When you need a fifth book, one has to go back. Which one?

The natural rule is to send back the book you opened longest ago. Many caches in programming libraries work that way, so it feels like the safe answer. But a database makes this choice thousands of times a second, and there that rule costs too much. And one big job that leafs through every book once can clear the desk of everything useful.

Pages, tuples and heap files cut a table into 8 KB pages, and every query reads pages. Reading one from a drive takes over a hundred times longer than reading it from memory. In this lesson, we'll build the database's own desk, the buffer pool, and watch PostgreSQL decide which page leaves. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a desk with room for four books, and a rule that sounded right: send back the one you opened longest ago. A database needs more than that. Pins keep pages in use where they are, the clock sweep picks a victim without reordering a list on every read, and a ring stops one big scan from clearing the desk.

If you can reach a PostgreSQL database, put EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) in front of any query and read the Buffers: line. Run it twice, and watch reads turn into hits.

Next, we'll stop reading every page to find one row, and find out how a tree of pages only three levels deep can find any of a million rows.

compare.title: LRU vs CLOCK on a hit

a.label: LRU
a.title: every hit reorders a list
a.html: // accessOrder = true: get() moves the entry to the end val lru = LinkedHashMap<Int, Frame>(16, 0.75f, true) fun hit(pageId: Int): Frame? = synchronized(lru) { lru[pageId] // a write to the shared list on every read } fun victim(): Frame = synchronized(lru) { lru.values.first { it.pinCount == 0 } // least recently used, unpinned }

b.label: CLOCK
b.title: a hit bumps one counter
b.html: fun hit(f: Frame) { f.pinCount++ f.usageCount = minOf(f.usageCount + 1, 5) // touches only this frame } fun victim(): Frame { // the lab adds a give-up rule while (true) { val f = frames[hand] hand = (hand + 1) % frames.size if (f.pinCount > 0) continue if (f.usageCount == 0) return f f.usageCount-- } }

compare.note: LRU throws out pages in exact order of last use, but it pays for that on every hit: the shared list changes on each read, under one lock. CLOCK pays on misses instead. The hand does a little work only when a frame is needed, and a hit touches nothing but its own frame. Databases read far more often than they evict, so that trade wins. PostgreSQL goes further, and updates the pin and usage counts with one compare-and-swap, so a hit takes no lock at all.

worked.title: Find out what's in shared_buffers, and how well it works

steps.say: Start with what the pool holds. This query from the pg_buffercache docs counts frames per table in the current database. Here, payments fills 1,280 frames (all its pages), and settlements holds only its 94-page ring.
steps.code: SELECT n.nspname, c.relname, count(*) AS buffers FROM pg_buffercache b JOIN pg_class c ON b.relfilenode = pg_relation_filenode(c.oid) AND b.reldatabase IN (0, (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database())) JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace GROUP BY n.nspname, c.relname ORDER BY 3 DESC LIMIT 5;

steps.say: Then measure how often reads hit. pg_statio_user_tables counts table pages found in the pool (heap_blks_hit) and pages that had to be read (heap_blks_read) since its numbers were last reset.
steps.code: SELECT relname, heap_blks_read, heap_blks_hit, round(100.0 * heap_blks_hit / nullif(heap_blks_hit + heap_blks_read, 0), 1) AS hit_pct FROM pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY heap_blks_read + heap_blks_hit DESC;

steps.say: Read the result with the lesson in mind. payments hits about 91% of the time after one cold read and a few warm scans. settlements sits at about 57% here, and that number includes building and vacuuming the table. Its big scans read through a ring, so its own pages are expected to miss.

Decide what a low hit rate means before you touch shared_buffers. A low rate on a table the app reads by key means its busy pages don't fit, or something keeps flushing them (look for index scans over huge ranges). A low rate on a table that's mostly read whole is normal. And a "read" may still have come from the OS page cache, so check the I/O timings in EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) before you decide the drive is slow.

lab.title: Build a buffer pool with pins and a clock sweep
steps: Read DiskManager.kt. It's complete: an interface that the tests fake in memory, and a FileDiskManager over a real file. Then read the Frame class at the top of BufferPool.kt.
Run the tests once. All 13 fail.
Write victim(): take a frame from free if there is one. Otherwise sweep with hand, using PostgreSQL's rules from the stepper, and give up after capacity pinned frames in a row.

Write fetch. On a hit, pin the frame and add one usage (at most MAX_USAGE). On a miss, get a victim, write its old page back if it's dirty, remove it from the page table, read the new page and set the frame up (pin 1, usage 1, clean).
Write unpin (dirty is sticky), newPage (victim first, then disk.allocatePage(), zeroed, pinned, dirty) and flushAll.
Run the tests until all 13 pass. The CLOCK tests check exact victims, so trace the stepper if one fails.
hints: A private evict(frame) helper that writes back a dirty page and removes it from the page table keeps fetch and newPage short.

Move the hand forward on every step, including the step that picks the victim, so the next sweep starts right past it. The test "pattern 1,2,3,1,4 evicts page 2" also checks where the next sweep starts.
In newPage, call victim() before disk.allocatePage(). If every frame is pinned, the exception must leave the disk untouched.
DiskManager always copies all 4,096 bytes, whatever the buffer's position, so pass frame.data as it is. To zero a frame, fill frame.data.array() with 0.

drill.title: Write the clock sweep from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write fun victim(): Frame for a pool with frames, hand, and a pinCount and usageCount on each frame. Follow PostgreSQL's rules, including the one that gives up when every frame is pinned. Then answer: why does a pinned frame keep its usage count?

answer.html: fun victim(): Frame { var tries = frames.size // pinned frames we may pass in a row while (true) { val f = frames[hand] hand = (hand + 1) % frames.size // always move on, even past the victim if (f.pinCount == 0) { if (f.usageCount == 0) return f // unpinned and out of credit: evict it f.usageCount-- // second chance, one credit less tries = frames.size } else if (--tries == 0) { throw NoFreeFrameException() // a whole lap of pinned frames } } } // A pinned page is in use right now, so it is the opposite of a good victim. // Taking its credits away would make it leave sooner the moment it is unpinned.

recap: A buffer pool is a fixed set of page-sized frames plus a page table. A hit costs no trip to the drive; a miss reads the page into a frame that the eviction rule picks.
fetch pins and unpin releases. A pinned frame is never evicted, and pins that are never released use up the pool until a miss has nowhere to go.
unpin(dirty = true) marks the page dirty, and the flag is sticky. A dirty victim is written back exactly once before its frame is reused; a clean one is dropped.
PostgreSQL's clock sweep keeps a usage count per frame (1 on load, plus 1 per pin, at most 5). The hand skips pinned frames, lowers the others, and evicts the first unpinned frame at 0.
A sequential scan of a table bigger than a quarter of shared_buffers uses a small ring of frames, so it can't flood the pool. An index scan over a huge range gets no ring.

The limit: PostgreSQL reads through the OS page cache, so a page can be cached twice; start shared_buffers near 25% of RAM. InnoDB and RocksDB use O_DIRECT instead, and PostgreSQL 18's asynchronous reads (io_method = worker by default; Docker blocks io_uring) are its first step that way.

explain.prompt: A friend asks why PostgreSQL doesn't keep shared_buffers in least-recently-used (LRU) order, since LRU is "the best" rule. Explain what PostgreSQL does instead and why, including what protects the pool from a giant nightly scan.
explain.answer: An exact LRU has to move a page to the front of a shared list on every hit. So every read becomes a write to one structure under a lock, and with many backends that lock becomes the bottleneck. PostgreSQL uses a clock sweep instead. Each frame has a usage count that goes up by one on each pin, up to 5. When it needs a frame, a hand walks round the pool, skips pinned frames, lowers the count of the others, and takes the first unpinned frame at zero. A hit only updates the frame's own counter, with one atomic instruction. For the nightly scan, neither LRU nor the clock would be enough on its own, because a scan touches millions of pages once. So PostgreSQL gives a sequential scan of a table bigger than a quarter of shared_buffers a small ring of frames. The scan keeps reusing those, and the busy pages stay.

deeper.html:
Smarter rules. CLOCK and LRU both look only at how recently a page was used, roughly. Two classic improvements look at how often, too. LRU-K (O'Neil, O'Neil and Weikum, 1993) evicts the page whose K-th most recent use is oldest, so a page touched once by a scan, with no second use, goes first. 2Q (Johnson and Shasha, 1994) puts new pages in a small trial queue and only promotes pages that are used again. Both resist sequential flooding without special cases. PostgreSQL's usage count, which a page earns by being pinned again and again, gets part of the same effect, and the ring buffers handle the rest.

Why not mmap? Mapping the data file into memory and letting the kernel load pages looks like a free buffer pool. The CIDR 2022 paper by Crotty, Leis and Pavlo explains why databases that tried it backed off. The kernel can write a dirty page back at any time, which breaks the rule that the WAL record must reach the drive first. A page fault blocks the thread, with no way to start the read early. An I/O error arrives as a SIGBUS signal instead of an error code. And under memory pressure the kernel's eviction becomes the bottleneck: a single kswapd thread does it, and every core must drop its cached copies of the old page addresses (TLB shootdowns). MongoDB's original MMAPv1 storage engine was deprecated in 2015 and removed in 2019. The paper's advice is to use mmap only when the data fits in memory and is only ever read.

Asynchronous I/O in more detail. With io_method = worker, backends put read requests in shared memory and the I/O workers pick them up. So one scan keeps many reads in flight, and merges neighbouring pages into one larger read (io_combine_limit, 128 kB by default). effective_io_concurrency limits how many reads one backend keeps in flight; PostgreSQL 18 raised its default from 1 to 16. Besides sequential scans and VACUUM, asynchronous reads serve bitmap heap scans, which read the rows an index has pointed at in page order. The pg_aios view lists the I/Os in flight. This is also why the ring for a sequential scan grew in PostgreSQL 18: frames that are still being read can't be reused yet, so the ring needs room for them. PostgreSQL 19, at release candidate as this is written, adjusts the number of I/O workers between io_min_workers and io_max_workers, and adds an IO option to EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Skipping the kernel's cache. Facebook's paper on MyRocks, a version of MySQL that keeps its data in RocksDB (a storage engine Facebook started), gives one more reason engines use O_DIRECT. With the kernel's cache in the way, Linux spent 2 to 3 GB of its own memory per terabyte of data files, and direct I/O cut that by over 80%. PostgreSQL does have an O_DIRECT switch, debug_io_direct, but its docs say it currently lowers performance and is meant for developers' tests. Andy Pavlo, who teaches databases at Carnegie Mellon University, calls PostgreSQL the only major database system still relying on the OS page cache, and sees PostgreSQL 18's asynchronous reads as the start of its path away from it.

Don't give shared_buffers everything. A bigger pool isn't always faster. Because PostgreSQL reads through the OS page cache, a 48 GB pool on a 64 GB server leaves little room for the OS cache, for sorting (work_mem) and for connections, and many pages end up cached twice anyway. Start near 25% of RAM, and measure hit rates and shared read counts before you change it. Oracle's buffer cache, sized by DB_CACHE_SIZE, is the same structure under another name.
